Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00770

There was a major objective reason why ʿUmar became especially associated with this kind of flexible legal reasoning. There was also, of course, a personal factor: ʿUmar himself had a flexible and practical mind.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00771
During the twenty years of ʿUmar’s caliphate, the Arab conquests brought the Arabs face to face with entirely new conditions in the conquered lands.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00772

They now encountered situations, questions, and problems that had never arisen in the life they had known in the Arabian Peninsula. To deal with them, they had to apply Islamic law with skill, flexibility, and creativity. They needed rulings for circumstances they had never faced before and had never previously needed to regulate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00773
This is what we mean by the objective factor.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00774

The Arab conquerors suddenly had to deal with new financial, administrative, organizational, military, social, and legal questions. They faced types of disputes unknown in their earlier, simpler society, as well as new questions of personal status.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00775
Did the two main sources of Islamic law—the Qurʾān and the Sunnah—contain detailed ready-made rulings for every one of these matters?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00775
Of course not.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00776
No body of law, whether divine or human, can contain a detailed text for every new situation that life will ever produce.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00777
So there was only one way to apply Islamic law to these new circumstances: the use of reasoned judgment, or ijtihād.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00778

The Arabs responsible for governing the conquered lands therefore turned to this new source of legal judgment and used it extensively. Arab historical works and the large body of legal literature contain countless examples of rulings reached through rational reflection based on the general principles of Islamic law.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00779
2 — The School of the People of Opinion
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00780
Out of the practical use of this legal method grew a distinct school known as the school of the “People of Opinion.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00781

It had become recognizable as a school with its own clear features by the middle of the first Islamic century, and its influence spread widely among jurists and judges during the first half of the second.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00782
It had several distinguishing features.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00783

First, its scholars did not limit themselves to giving legal judgments on real cases placed before them. They also imagined cases that had not actually happened and tried to work out what legal judgment should apply to each hypothetical situation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00784
Second, some of its representatives did not feel obliged to search first for a hadith from the Prophet before using their own judgment.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00785

Some members of this school would even refuse to base a ruling on a prophetic hadith when a hadith directly matching the case was available. Their reason was the growing doubt, after some time had passed since the Prophet, about the reliability of hadith reports transmitted through chains of narrators.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00786
“Al-Baghdādī attributed the rejection of acting on hadith to the Kharijites in his book Uṣūl al-Dīn.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00787
There was another striking feature of the School of Opinion: it was especially widespread and firmly rooted in Iraq.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00788
Aḥmad Amīn gives three reasons for this.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00789
First, two of its most famous figures, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd and later Abū Ḥanīfa, lived in Iraq and helped spread the use of personal judgment and analogical reasoning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00790

Second, Ibn Khaldūn noted that the people of “the Hijaz transmitted more hadith than the people of Iraq, because Medina was the home of the Hijra and the gathering place of the Companions. Those who later moved from there to Iraq were largely occupied with the great military campaigns.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
en-ref-V2-39-1
Third:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00791

“Iraq was a land of cities” and “had been deeply influenced by Persian and Greek civilization. Urban life constantly presents the law with many detailed questions requiring rulings, to a degree that cannot be compared with a largely nomadic region. Once this was combined with the amount of hadith that had reached Iraq, the result was inevitably a greater use of personal judgment.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00792

This third reason is what we had in mind earlier when we said that intellectual conflict in this period was deeply connected with the different social environments found across the Arab-Islamic world.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00793
This will become even clearer when we turn to the School of the People of Hadith.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00794
3 — The School of the People of Hadith
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00795
This school arose in response to the School of Opinion and took the opposite position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00796

Its scholars rejected the use of personal opinion in legal judgment. If a case arose that required a ruling and they could not find one in the Qurʾān, they searched for a prophetic hadith that applied to it. If they could not find such a hadith, they stopped and gave no ruling on the case.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00797

Some took this position so far that they placed hadith above the Qurʾān itself. Some jurists of the second Islamic century went even further and argued that the Sunnah—that is, prophetic hadith—could abrogate rulings in the Qurʾān.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00798
The features of this school were almost the exact opposite of those we described in the School of Opinion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00799

If the School of Opinion arose, became established, and spread in Iraq for the three reasons just given, then the School of Hadith arose, became established, and spread in the Hijaz for the same reasons in reverse.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00800

Its best-known figures, such as Imam Mālik, lived in the Hijaz, the land in which the Prophet himself had lived. Hadith was also far more abundant there than in Iraq. And finally, the Hijaz was a largely “nomadic region” that had not been strongly affected by “Persian and Greek civilization,” to use Aḥmad Amīn’s explanation quoted above.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00801
The difference between the two schools can also be seen in their attitude toward hypothetical cases.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00802
The School of Opinion was willing to imagine situations that had never actually happened and then use reasoned judgment to work out the legal ruling that would apply.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00803
The School of Hadith strongly disliked this practice. Its scholars refused to answer questions unless they concerned events that had really taken place.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00804
At first, the conflict between these two opposing tendencies was mainly a conflict over law.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00805
But it became increasingly intense and eventually expanded into a much broader intellectual struggle.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00806
Later, we find each tendency taking a position in the major intellectual conflicts of the time that closely matched the position it had already taken in the legal debate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00807

From the legal tradition of the People of Opinion came intellectual figures such as al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. It was from his teaching circle in the mosque of Basra that the well-known rationalist school of the Muʿtazila eventually emerged.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00808

The People of Hadith, by contrast, entered the broader intellectual struggle with the same conservative attitude they had shown in legal matters. From their traditionalist school came figures such as Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, who strongly opposed the principles of the Muʿtazila.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00809
B — The Rise of the Arab Sciences
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00810
1 — Arab Sciences or Islamic Sciences?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00811
Would it not be more accurate to call the sciences that arose in the early Islamic period “Islamic sciences” rather than “Arab sciences”?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00812

After all, their development was directly connected with Islam—with its foundational texts, its leading figures, and the events of its early history. This was true both of the subjects these sciences studied and of the forces and purposes behind their emergence.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00813
The question is entirely reasonable.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00814
We have nevertheless chosen to call them the “Arab sciences,” even though we are fully aware of this historical fact and of how difficult it is to draw a sharp line between the two names.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00815

From the moment Islam entered Arab life, it became one of the forces shaping that life. It became part of its events, interactions, conflicts, and cultural developments. In this way, Islam also became one of the most important forces shaping the course of Arab history across the different areas of social life.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00816
So when we choose the term “Arab sciences,” we do not mean to deny, ignore, or move beyond this fact.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00817
The distinction we are making is a different one.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00818

Some sciences arose within the specifically Arab environment and dealt directly with the Arabic language, or with people who had lived through Islam’s beginnings and its earliest movement and events in its Arab birthplace.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00819

Other sciences arose later in a much broader environment, where Arab life interacted with the life of many different peoples. These later sciences were the product of a much wider process of cultural exchange and interaction.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00820
But distinguishing between these two kinds of science does not mean creating an artificial division inside the culture we call Arab-Islamic culture.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00821

We can already state our position on this clearly. We will need to return to it in greater detail when we discuss Arab-Islamic philosophy, because there too we will face the question of whether it should instead be called “Islamic philosophy.” Our position there will be the same as it is here.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00822

Put briefly, the culture produced by the living, dialectical relationship between Arab life and Islamic life, between Arab thought and Islamic thought, and between language and the thought expressed through that language, is an Arab-Islamic culture.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00823
It cannot be divided neatly into something purely Arab, something purely Islamic, and something that is a mixture of the two.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00824
Nor can it be divided between works produced by thinkers of Arab ancestry and works produced by Muslim thinkers of non-Arab ancestry.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00825
They all belong to the same culture.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00826

All of them developed their thought through the Arabic language—with its linguistic, expressive, and intellectual patterns. And in their cultural work, across its many different fields, they were all responding to the questions of a particular society: its social, political, and intellectual problems.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00827
They all lived within that society, and they all formed their view of the world through its historical reality and its pattern of social relations.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00828

The sciences we are discussing here, which we have chosen to call Arab rather than Islamic sciences, dealt with the Arabic language, its rules, and its literature; with Arab history before and after Islam; with the life of the Prophet and the lives of his Companions and successors; with reports of the Arab conquests; with the language of the Qurʾān and prophetic hadith and the meanings carried by that language; and with the study of hadith itself, including its transmission and its transmitters.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00829
Their purpose also included using the language of the Qurʾān and hadith to draw out their teachings on belief and law.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00830

More precisely, by the “Arab sciences” we mean those sciences connected most directly with the Arabic language itself: grammar, rhetoric, literature, history, Qurʾānic interpretation, hadith, and Islamic law, including both jurisprudence and the principles of jurisprudence.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00831
All of these disciplines depended on knowledge of how Arabic works, because Arabic was the sole language through which the teachings of Islam were expressed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00832
We are not inventing the term “Arab sciences,” nor do we claim to be doing so. It was used in earlier times as well.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00833
Al-Khwārizmī, for example, says while describing his book Mafātīḥ al-ʿUlūm:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00834
“I divided it into two parts: one for the sciences of religious law and the Arab sciences connected with them, and another for the sciences of foreign peoples, including the Greeks and others.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00835
Our reason for discussing these “Arab sciences” here is limited to one point.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00836

Their rise in the early Islamic period, and especially during the Umayyad period, became a starting point for a wider movement of cultural development. That cultural development was itself one of the clearest expressions of the deeper changes taking place in the basic structures of the society ruled by the Islamic caliphate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00837
The rise of these sciences answered the needs created by that wider development.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00838
The expanding state needed more organized forms of knowledge to support its economic, social, administrative, and financial organization.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00839

At the same time, the Arab-Islamic conquests had spread across many countries and peoples. These populations now had to adapt to the language of the conquerors—to speak it and understand its meanings according to some organized set of rules.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00840
There was also another problem.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00841

As non-Arab peoples began speaking Arabic, and as Arabs mixed with speakers of other languages, it soon became clear that Arabic itself could lose much of its original purity, even among Arabs. Many Arabs were now living in new geographical and social surroundings far from the environment in which their language had originally developed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00842
From an Islamic point of view, this created a serious danger.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00843
Muslims—including Arab Muslims—could gradually lose the ability to understand the beliefs and laws of Islam from what were then their only sources: the Qurʾān and the Sunnah.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00844

Those sources used forms of expression regarded as among the highest achievements of Arabic in style, structure, and composition. Their contents also included metaphysical ideas, theories of knowledge, and legal concepts.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00845

In the Qurʾān, these were often expressed in an artistic, suggestive, and indirect form. At other times, they were expressed very compactly, in language capable of carrying several possible meanings and intentions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00846
There was an additional difficulty.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00847

At first, the texts of the Qurʾān and hadith were not generally available in written form. What had been written down circulated among only a limited number of the Companions. Most of these texts were preserved through oral transmission by people who had heard them from the Prophet.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00848
Those people later scattered across different lands with the armies of conquest. Some were killed in those wars. Others gradually died, one after another, in widely separated regions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00849
All these factors, working together, created the need for the new sciences.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00850
First came the need to establish the rules of Arabic grammar.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00851
Second came the need to organize knowledge of the language’s rhetorical and expressive features.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00852
Then came the need to interpret the language of the Qurʾān and explain its teachings on belief and law in the light of this organized linguistic knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00853

There was also the need to collect prophetic hadith, verify different reports, distinguish one transmitter’s account from another, and study the life of each transmitter in order to judge how trustworthy that person was, whether he had actually been connected with the Prophet during the Prophet’s lifetime, and so on.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00854
The early rise of these sciences created an active and energetic cultural life.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00855
This helped the growing intellectual movement—which was itself developing alongside political conflict—gain access to a body of knowledge that had at least begun to be classified and organized.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00856
At this stage, however, the classification was still basic and the organization still primitive. The full elements of specialized scientific study had not yet developed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00857

That kind of organization becomes possible only when knowledge has advanced and expanded enough for people to feel the need to classify it according to a common subject and to bring related material together in a coherent way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00858
The new sciences were still too young at this early stage of Islam for such classification to be complete.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00859

For that reason, the “Arab sciences” remained closely intertwined. Clear boundaries between them did not emerge until the great flowering of Arab-Islamic culture in the late second Islamic century, during the early Abbasid period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00860
For the same reason, the intellectual questions produced by political conflict did not yet take the form of a clearly organized science with its own method.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00861
That development came only in the later period we have just mentioned.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00862
We are speaking here specifically of the questions that would eventually form the science of kalām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00863

From the beginning of the Umayyad period, debate had already arisen over the caliphate, the person who commits a major sin, and the meaning of faith. Later came debates over divine decree and human responsibility for action, followed by metaphysical questions about the attributes of God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00864
But for a long time, the intellectual material produced by all these debates remained scattered.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00865
It had not yet been brought together into a single independent discipline with a clearly defined subject and its own rational method.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00866
That happened only later, when philosophical thinking itself became the starting point and basic framework of Arab-Islamic thought across its different fields of activity.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-00867
This was the Abbasid period associated with the age of al-Maʾmūn.
